transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi... yeah, thank you. I just... I really didn't know where else to go, honestly. I came in because I just can't stop this awful feeling that I'm, well, that I'm a complete danger to the people around me. And a massive disappointment. 

I'm a nurse, you know, and I worked so hard to get through my college courses and get my license so young, but lately... well, there was this one incident at work. A near-miss. Nobody actually got hurt, thank God, but I just keep replaying the whole shift over and over and over in my head every single day. I analyze every little thing I did leading up to it, and it just completely proves to me that I'm not meant to do this. I'm not meant to be a nurse at all. 

I try to tell myself it was just a near-miss, that people make mistakes, but it feels so much heavier than that, you know? It feels like this deep, fundamental flaw in who I am, like I'm just going to end up seriously hurting someone if I keep trying to do my job. It's gotten to the point where I look at my family, my coworkers, my patients... and I just keep thinking that everyone would honestly be so much better off without me around. Without me getting in the way or messing things up or putting people at risk. It's just this constant, suffocating guilt that follows me everywhere, and I just don't know how to carry it anymore.
Have you been having persistent, intrusive thoughts or mental images related to the incident at work, even when you're not actively trying to think about it?

Um... I don't think so? Not like... not like they just pop into my head completely out of nowhere, if that's what you mean. It's not like I'm seeing flashes of the hospital room or the equipment when I'm just trying to eat breakfast or something. It's more... it's more that I'm the one bringing it up. I just sit there and make myself think about it. 

Like, yesterday afternoon, I was just sitting in my room, looking at my old textbooks—I kept all my books from my college courses because I thought I'd need them for reference, since I got my license so young and I wanted to be totally, one-hundred-percent prepared for anything—and I just started going through the entire shift minute by minute in my head again. I'll just sit there and go, 'Okay, at 10 AM I checked the chart, at 10:15 I did this,' just trying to pinpoint the exact second where I proved how completely unfit I am for this job. 

So it's not really the memories forcing themselves on me when I'm trying to do other things. It's more that I *am* trying to think about it, constantly, because I feel like I have to. I feel like if I stop thinking about it, or if I try to just distract myself and watch a movie, I'm just being irresponsible all over again. It's like I need to punish myself by remembering exactly how badly I almost messed up. I just... I can't let myself forget it, so I just keep digging back into it on purpose. I don't know if that's what you meant, but yeah, it's mostly just me doing it to myself.
Have you been feeling this same level of guilt and worthlessness most of the day, nearly every day, even when you're not actively thinking about the incident at work?

Yeah... yeah, it really is. It's all day, every single day. I know I sort of said this right when I sat down, but that's really the whole reason I came in today, because I just can't stop feeling like I'm this... this walking danger to people, and just a massive disappointment to everyone who believed in me. And it's not even just when I'm actively sitting there dissecting that shift, like I was telling you about. It's literally all the time. 

I'll wake up in the morning, and before I even open my eyes or remember what day it is, I already have this awful pit in my stomach. I'll be doing something totally mindless, like brushing my teeth or trying to make a bowl of cereal, and I just feel so incredibly heavy and... and useless. It's like that one near-miss didn't just stay at the hospital, you know? It followed me home and now it just colors everything I do. It just completely proves to me that I'm not meant to be a nurse, but it goes deeper than that now. It feels like it proves I'm just fundamentally broken or bad at everything. 

Even when I'm just sitting in the living room with my family, and we're just watching a show or something and nobody is even talking about work, I can't even focus on the TV. I'm just looking at them and thinking about how much easier their lives would be if they didn't have to worry about me. I just sit there absolutely convinced that everyone would be so much better off without me around to mess things up. So, yeah, even when I'm not actively trying to punish myself by thinking about the hospital or my patients, that feeling of being a total disappointment is just... it's just always there. It never really turns off.
Have you lost interest or stopped enjoying activities that you used to like, such as hobbies, spending time with loved ones, or watching your favorite shows?

Yeah... yeah, it’s honestly exactly like that. It’s actually really sad when I stop and think about it, because I used to be someone who had so many things going on outside of work and school. You know, because I pushed myself so hard with my college courses to get my nursing license so early, I really had to build in ways to decompress and separate myself from the stress. 

I used to clear my head by jogging—I had this whole three-mile route I’d do around my neighborhood every evening just to shake off the day. Or I’d be knitting. I used to love knitting, I actually made this huge, complicated cable-knit blanket for my mom last year. And I loved cooking, too, like finding these really intricate recipes online and spending hours in the kitchen just focusing on chopping and measuring, just to give my brain a break. Or even just reading for fun after class, like big fantasy novels that had absolutely nothing to do with medicine or the real world. 

But now... I don't know, it’s like a switch just flipped in my brain. I look at my running shoes by the door, or the half-finished scarf sitting on my nightstand, and I feel absolutely nothing. I don't have any desire to pick any of it up. Now, I basically just come home, and I just sit on my bed in my scrubs. I don't even bother changing out of my work clothes half the time because it just feels like too much effort, and I just sit there. I look at the books I used to love, or think about trying to make a nice dinner, and I just... I can't make myself care about any of it anymore. It’s all just completely lost its appeal. I just sit there in my scrubs staring at the wall, and I can't even force myself to find an ounce of joy in the things that used to make me so happy.
Have you had any thoughts about ending your life or hurting yourself as a way to escape these feelings?

I... I mean, I don't have a plan. I really don't. It's not like I'm sitting there figuring out how to actually do something to myself, like hoarding pills or planning out some specific way to end it. I know I couldn't do that to my family. I mean, my mom was so proud of me when I passed my boards, and my dad practically told everyone in our neighborhood that his eighteen-year-old daughter was already a registered nurse. I couldn't do that to them, actively hurt them like that. 

But... but at the same time, the thoughts are just... they're there. It's more like this constant, heavy wish that I could just... not be here anymore. Like, when I finally do fall asleep, there's this moment right before I drift off where I just think, 'It would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up tomorrow.' Because if I don't wake up, I don't have to go back to the hospital, I don't have to face the other nurses who probably know how incompetent I am, and I don't have to worry about making another mistake that could actually kill someone next time. 

It's just this overwhelming feeling of wanting to disappear. Sometimes I'll be sitting in my car in the driveway after a shift, just staring at the steering wheel for like twenty minutes, and I just imagine what it would be like if I could just evaporate. Just cease to exist, without the messy part of actually dying. Because if I wasn't here, I couldn't mess anything up again. I wouldn't be this huge burden, this walking disaster just waiting to ruin someone's life because I checked a chart wrong or hesitated for a second too long. So, no, I'm not planning to kill myself, but... but wanting to just be gone, wanting to just stop existing so I can't do any more damage... yeah, I think about that a lot. Probably more than I should.
Before this recent incident at work, have you ever experienced a period of time when you felt this same level of guilt, hopelessness, or loss of interest in things you used to enjoy?

Well, um... I guess if I'm being completely honest, the incident at work is what really pushed it over the edge and made me realize I needed to talk to someone, but... but no, it didn't just start with that near-miss. It's actually been going on for a while now. I think I've been feeling this way, just this constant, heavy feeling of not being good enough and not enjoying anything, for about a year and two months now. 

It really started right after I graduated high school. Because, you know, I was doing all these accelerated programs, so I was graduating high school and then immediately jumping into college classes and starting full-time clinic work all at the exact same time. And I remember everyone telling me how amazing it was, how I was so far ahead of everyone my age, and I just felt this enormous pressure to keep it all together and prove them right. But instead, almost as soon as that schedule started, I just started feeling so incredibly drained and hollow. Like, I'd go to my college courses and take all these intense science prerequisites, and then I'd go straight to the clinic for a full shift, and I just felt like I was drowning, but I couldn't tell anyone because I was supposed to be this prodigy, you know? 

So, yeah, it started back then, about fourteen months ago. That's when I first noticed I didn't want to go running anymore, and that's when the guilt started creeping in, this feeling that I was fooling everyone and that I wasn't actually smart enough or capable enough to be doing what I was doing. The incident at work just... it just confirmed all those terrible things I'd already been thinking about myself for over a year.
